title: Raman and UVN+LWIR LIBS detection system for in-situ surface chemical identification
author: Yang, Bower, et al.

steps.title: Assemble laser and LWIR optics
steps.instruction: Install the Q‑switched Nd:YAG laser (Quantel CFR400) set to 10 Hz repetition and 75–110 mJ pulse energy; place a plano‑convex focusing lens to direct the beam onto the sample positioned 1 m from the instrument; mount a 6‑inch Cassegrain telescope to collect plasma emission and focus it into the input slit of a modified SP2150 Czerny–Turner monochromator (input focal length 150 mm, grating 30 grooves mm⁻¹, output focal length 50 mm); set the input slit width to 0.5 mm; replace the original output focusing lens with a flat mirror and add a 50 mm focal‑length lens to image the slit onto a liquid‑nitrogen‑cooled linear LWIR array (300 HgCdTe pixels, 50 µm pitch/height); ensure the array analog output is digitized to 16‑bit values.

steps.title: Assemble VIS/NIR collection optics
steps.instruction: Collect the visible/NIR plasma emission with two 75 mm‑diameter lenses (first f = 1 m to collimate, second f = 100 mm to focus) into a 200 µm core, 0.22 NA multimode fiber; connect the fiber to a CCS200 spectrometer (Thorlabs) covering 200–1000 nm.

steps.title: Configure instrument timing parameters
steps.instruction: Using the PC, send the desired LWIR delay time and integration time, and the Vis/NIR spectrometer delay time, to the microcontroller; transmit the Vis/NIR integration time directly to the CCS200 via USB; when the laser fires, the microcontroller receives the synchronization pulse and issues trigger pulses to the CCS200 and LWIR array after the specified delays, then stops LWIR integration after the set integration period; typical settings are LWIR delay = 20 µs, LWIR integration = 42 µs, Vis/NIR delay = 3 µs, Vis/NIR integration = 10 µs.

steps.title: Measure background and calibration spectra
steps.instruction: Before each measurement set, record a dark background with the LWIR array using the same integration time but without firing the laser; then acquire a spectrum of a ~600 °C blackbody source to map pixel‑to‑pixel responsivity; use these two measurements for a 2‑point non‑uniformity correction of the LWIR data.

steps.title: Acquire sample UVN and LWIR spectra
steps.instruction: Place the solid sample (no preparation required) within the instrument’s field of view; scan the surface as needed; fire a single laser pulse to generate a micro‑plasma; within seconds, collect simultaneous UVN (Vis/NIR) spectra from the CCS200 and mid‑IR spectra from the LWIR linear array; process the data to obtain atomic and molecular composition of the target.

description: Current advances in laser-based optical spectroscopy demonstrate the effectiveness of non-contact methods for in situ and remote sensing of surface deposit composition on planetary bodies. For example, Raman spectroscopy has been chosen for in situ planetary NASA missions because it is an information-rich, non-contact, non-destructive method for identifying and characterizing inorganic and organic compounds in a wide variety of planetary materials. Laser Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) in the Ultra Violet/Visible/Near-IR (UVN) spectral range is a powerful analytical tool that facilitates the interpretation of Raman spectroscopic data by providing additional detail in elemental chemistry. Both LIBS and Raman spectroscopy are part of the payloads of NASA's Perseverance rover and on ESA's ExoMars rover [1,2]. However, some challenges remain. For Raman spectroscopy, the spectral signature signals are usually very weak and the sensitivity and accuracy of the surface measurements are strongly influenced by surface shape, roughness, composition irregularity and background emissions (e.g. fluoresce from the surface) [3]. Another challenge for Raman spectroscopy is in distinguishing diagnostic peaks in samples of mixed composition, common for compositionally heterogeneous targets in natural environments. Structural commonalities between compounds can result in similar peak positions of many co-occurring substrates and organic compounds, resulting in the misinterpretation of spectra and possible misidentification [4]. And though UVN LIBS helps to clarify some of ambiguity in the Raman spectra, it is an atomic spectroscopic technology that reveals no information on molecular structures [5].
